# Exercise 2.4 — Imputation {#sec-imputation}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## In R or in Python
Pick a tab and stay in it. The two tabs are the same exercise — the same
sections, the same tasks, the same numbers — so complete either one.
:::

## Objectives

By the end of this exercise you will be able to:

- quantify how much data you would lose by dropping every incomplete row;
- fill missing values with a mean or a median, and measure what that does to
  the spread of the column;
- say why the median is the safer default for a skewed variable;
- explain why imputing the inputs of a derived feature does not fill the
  derived feature;
- argue for leaving a value missing rather than inventing one.

## Why this, here

@sec-cleaning left the extract clean but incomplete. The missing-value codes
are now real missing values, which means they can finally be counted — and
something has to be decided about them, because most models will not accept a
missing value at all.

## Starting point

Each chapter stands alone, so the block below repeats @sec-cleaning's cleaning
in one go — the codes recognised, the labels standardised, the three
correctable heights fixed, the two impossible values admitted as missing, and
BMI derived.

:::::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

na_codes <- c("unknown", "?", "not recorded", "N/A", "-999")
num_cols <- c("age", "height_cm", "weight_kg", "systolic_BP")

gp <- read_csv("data/clinic_extract.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ if_else(as.character(.x) %in% na_codes,
                                        NA_character_, as.character(.x)))) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(num_cols), as.numeric),
         diabetes = as.integer(diabetes)) |>
  mutate(
    height_cm = if_else(height_cm < 3, height_cm * 100, height_cm),
    age       = if_else(age > 120, NA_real_, age),
    weight_kg = if_else(weight_kg > 300, NA_real_, weight_kg),
    sex = case_when(
      str_to_lower(str_trim(sex)) %in% c("male", "m")   ~ "Male",
      str_to_lower(str_trim(sex)) %in% c("female", "f") ~ "Female"),
    GP_practice = fct_lump_min(factor(GP_practice), min = 10,
                               other_level = "Other")
  ) |>
  mutate(BMI = weight_kg / (height_cm / 100)^2)

dim(gp)
```

Note that `BMI` is itself derived from two columns that have gaps, so it
inherits both — one of the things this exercise has to deal with.

#### How much is missing, and where

```{r}
print(colSums(is.na(gp[num_cols])))
cat("BMI missing:", sum(is.na(gp$BMI)), "\n")
cat("complete rows:", sum(complete.cases(gp)), "of", nrow(gp), "\n")
```

Note the arithmetic. The four numeric columns are missing 1, 12, 8 and 14
values — 35 in total — and `BMI` is missing 20 of its own, inherited from
height and weight. Yet only 134 of the 180 rows are complete. The count of
complete rows is lower than any single column's gap count, because the gaps
fall in different rows. This is the first argument against dropping incomplete
rows: the loss compounds across columns, and it compounds faster the more
columns you have.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Mean and median imputation

The idea is the simplest one available: put the column's own average where a
value is missing. It needs no model, no package, and one line.

```{r}
imp_mean <- gp |>
  mutate(across(all_of(num_cols),
                ~ if_else(is.na(.x), mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x)))

imp_median <- gp |>
  mutate(across(all_of(num_cols),
                ~ if_else(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x)))

cat("missing left, mean:  ", sum(is.na(imp_mean[num_cols])), "\n")
cat("missing left, median:", sum(is.na(imp_median[num_cols])), "\n")
```

`scikit-learn`'s `SimpleImputer` does the same job in the Python tab, and that
is the form you will meet again in @sec-pipeline-steps, where the imputer has
to be fitted on the training rows alone.

#### What it did to the spread

Thirty-five values across four columns have just been replaced by four
repeated numbers, so those rows now sit exactly on top of each other in each
column. The standard deviations must fall. Measure it rather than taking it on
trust:

```{r}
comparison <- data.frame(
  column    = num_cols,
  sd_before = sapply(gp[num_cols], sd, na.rm = TRUE),
  sd_mean   = sapply(imp_mean[num_cols], sd),
  sd_median = sapply(imp_median[num_cols], sd)
)
comparison$pct_change_mean <- round(
  100 * (comparison$sd_mean - comparison$sd_before) / comparison$sd_before, 1)
comparison
```

Every standard deviation shrank — by 0.3% for `age`, which was missing one
value, and by 4.0% for `systolic_BP`, which was missing fourteen. The size of
the shrinkage tracks how much of the column you invented.

That matters because a standard deviation is what a confidence interval is
built from: impute the mean into 8% of a column and every interval computed
from it afterwards is narrower than the evidence justifies. You have not added
information, but you have made the data look as though you had.

#### Why median, for this column

`BMI` is right-skewed. The mean is pulled upward by the heavier tail; the
median is not.

```{r}
cat("BMI mean  :", round(mean(gp$BMI, na.rm = TRUE), 2), "\n")
cat("BMI median:", round(median(gp$BMI, na.rm = TRUE), 2), "\n")
```

A gap of 0.35 of a BMI unit between the two. That is small here because the
skew is mild, and it is the right habit anyway: whichever you choose, every
filled-in value inherits it, so on a strongly skewed column the mean would put
a block of patients at a value most of the cohort sits below.

#### A derived feature does not impute itself

Here is the trap. `BMI` was computed from height and weight **before** the
imputation, so filling the gaps in those two columns does nothing to it — the
derived column still has every gap it started with.

```{r}
cat("BMI missing, before imputing:", sum(is.na(gp$BMI)), "\n")
cat("BMI missing, after imputing height and weight:",
    sum(is.na(imp_median$BMI)), "\n")
```

Twenty before, twenty after. Unchanged. The fix is to recompute the derived
column from the filled inputs, and the order matters: impute first, then
derive.

```{r}
imp_median <- imp_median |>
  mutate(BMI = weight_kg / (height_cm / 100)^2)

cat("BMI missing, after recomputing:", sum(is.na(imp_median$BMI)), "\n")
```

Zero. Note what those recomputed BMI values now are: a ratio of two numbers
that were themselves invented. The uncertainty does not announce itself — it is
buried one step further from the data than it was before.

Now colour the imputed rows, because a value at the median does not announce
itself in a histogram either — it lands inside the existing peak and disappears:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.6
imp_median |>
  mutate(source = if_else(is.na(gp$weight_kg) | is.na(gp$height_cm),
                          "imputed", "observed")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = BMI, fill = source)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(imputed = "#c0392b", observed = "grey40")) +
  labs(x = "BMI", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

Twenty red rows, all of them inside the existing peak. That is the honest
picture, and it is also the warning: had you not kept track of which rows you
filled, nothing in the finished column would tell you. A column of imputed
values looks exactly like a column of measurements. Record which is which — a
`BMI_was_missing` indicator costs one column and keeps the distinction
available to everything downstream.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Task 1 — What dropping costs

Dropping every incomplete row is the default in a surprising amount of
published analysis, usually silently. Quantify it.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
kept <- gp |> filter(______(gp))
cat(nrow(kept), "of", nrow(gp), "\n")
cat("lost:", round(100 * (1 - nrow(kept) / nrow(gp)), 1), "%\n")

# Did dropping change who is in the data?
cat(round(mean(gp$diabetes), 3), "\n")
cat(round(mean(kept$______), 3), "\n")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the function returning TRUE for rows with no missing value
anywhere. The last is the `diabetes` column, so you can compare its rate before
and after.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
kept <- gp |> filter(complete.cases(gp))
cat(nrow(kept), "of", nrow(gp), "\n")
cat("lost:", round(100 * (1 - nrow(kept) / nrow(gp)), 1), "%\n")

cat(round(mean(gp$diabetes), 3), "\n")
cat(round(mean(kept$diabetes), 3), "\n")
```

A quarter of the cohort goes — 134 rows kept of 180, 25.6% lost. The outcome
rate barely moves, from 0.233 to 0.224, which is what you expect when values
were blanked out at random — and is exactly what you cannot count on when they
were not.
:::
:::

### Task 2 — The categorical analogue

A mean is no use to a column of practice names. The usual substitute is the
most frequent category. Find it, and see how big it already is.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
mode_site <- names(sort(table(gp$GP_practice), decreasing = ______))[1]
mode_site

sum(gp$GP_practice == mode_site)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
You want the *largest* count first.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
mode_site <- names(sort(table(gp$GP_practice), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
mode_site

sum(gp$GP_practice == mode_site)
```

Bournbrook, with 49 of the 180 patients. Most-frequent-category imputation is
the categorical analogue of the mean, and it has the same defect in a sharper
form: it makes the commonest category commoner, which is precisely the
direction that hides a minority group. Filling a missing practice with
Bournbrook does not record ignorance, it records a guess that favours the
majority.
:::
:::

### Reflection

1. The four numeric columns were missing 1, 12, 8 and 14 values, yet 46 of the
   180 rows were incomplete. Explain the arithmetic to someone who has not seen
   the data, and say what it implies for a dataset with 50 columns.
2. Mean imputation shrank every standard deviation. Name one statistic you
   would report after imputing that would now be wrong, and say in which
   direction.
3. Imputing height and weight left `BMI` exactly as missing as before. Name
   another derived quantity in a clinical dataset where the same trap would
   apply.
4. Under what circumstance is leaving a value missing — and telling the reader
   it is missing — a better answer than any of the methods here?

### Stretch

#### Stretch 1 — Iterative imputation

Mean imputation ignores every other column. If a patient's `BMI` is missing but
their `age` and `systolic_BP` are recorded, those two carry information about
the likely `BMI`, and the mean throws it away. Iterative imputation uses it: it
models each column with missing values as a function of the other columns,
predicts the gaps, and repeats — each round using the previous round's filled-in
values — until the estimates settle.

It is a model, and it carries a model's assumptions: that the columns are
related in a way the imputer can represent, and that the missingness does not
itself depend on the value that is missing. For this dataset we happen to know
the second assumption holds, because `data/PROVENANCE.txt` records that values
were blanked out at random after the outcome was generated. On real data you
would not know that, and you would have to argue for it.

R's implementation is the [`mice` package](https://amices.org/mice/), whose
name is the method: Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations. It is not
used anywhere in this booklet, so treat this as reading rather than a cell to
run. Two things are worth knowing before you reach for it. Its default method
for a numeric column is predictive mean matching, which borrows a real observed
value from a similar patient rather than predicting a new one. And it is built
to produce *several* completed datasets rather than one, because the spread
between them is the measure of how uncertain each filled-in value was —
asking it for a single dataset throws away the thing it exists to give you.

The Python tab shows the scikit-learn equivalent,
[`IterativeImputer`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.impute.IterativeImputer.html),
if you want to see one run.

#### Stretch 2 — Make the imputation wrong on purpose
The values in this file were blanked out at random. Blank out `BMI` instead
for the patients with the highest `systolic_BP`, then impute with the mean and
compare the imputed values against the ones you deleted. You know the truth,
so you can measure the error — and see how an assumption of random missingness
fails when it is not true.

#### Stretch 3 — Does better imputation buy a better model?
Fit the same classifier on the mean-imputed and the median-imputed data and
compare the test-set accuracy. Form a view before you run it. Then consider how
much of any difference you would be willing to attribute to the imputer, given
that the comparison rests on one split.

### What you can and cannot now claim

You can say the extract is now complete: no model will refuse it, and you can
state exactly which values were observed and which you supplied, and by what
rule.

You cannot say the imputed values are correct. They are estimates, and the mean
and median versions are estimates that ignore every other column in the table.
You also cannot claim your downstream uncertainty is honest — the shrinkage you
measured is still there.

And once again, none of this was done safely. Every mean and median above was
computed from all 180 rows, including the rows you will later use to test. That
is @sec-pipeline-steps.

## Python

```{python}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

na_codes = ["unknown", "?", "not recorded", "N/A", "-999"]
num_cols = ["age", "height_cm", "weight_kg", "systolic_BP"]

gp_py = pd.read_csv("data/clinic_extract.csv",
                    keep_default_na=False, na_values=[""])
gp_py = gp_py.replace(na_codes, np.nan).replace(-999, np.nan)
for c in num_cols:
    gp_py[c] = pd.to_numeric(gp_py[c], errors="coerce")

gp_py.loc[gp_py.height_cm < 3, "height_cm"] *= 100
gp_py.loc[gp_py.age > 120, "age"] = np.nan
gp_py.loc[gp_py.weight_kg > 300, "weight_kg"] = np.nan

spelling = gp_py["sex"].str.strip().str.lower()
sex_clean = pd.Series(np.nan, index=gp_py.index, dtype="object")
sex_clean[spelling.isin(["male", "m"])]   = "Male"
sex_clean[spelling.isin(["female", "f"])] = "Female"
gp_py["sex"] = sex_clean

counts = gp_py["GP_practice"].value_counts()
rare = counts[counts < 10].index
gp_py["GP_practice"] = gp_py["GP_practice"].where(
    ~gp_py["GP_practice"].isin(rare), "Other")

gp_py["BMI"] = gp_py.weight_kg / (gp_py.height_cm / 100) ** 2

print(gp_py.shape)
```

Note that `BMI` is itself derived from two columns that have gaps, so it
inherits both — one of the things this exercise has to deal with.

#### How much is missing, and where

```{python}
print(gp_py[num_cols].isna().sum())
print("BMI missing:", int(gp_py["BMI"].isna().sum()))
print("complete rows:", gp_py.dropna().shape[0], "of", gp_py.shape[0])
```

Note the arithmetic. The four numeric columns are missing 1, 12, 8 and 14
values — 35 in total — and `BMI` is missing 20 of its own, inherited from
height and weight. Yet only 134 of the 180 rows are complete. The count of
complete rows is lower than any single column's gap count, because the gaps
fall in different rows. This is the first argument against dropping incomplete
rows: the loss compounds across columns, and it compounds faster the more
columns you have.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Mean and median imputation

The idea is the simplest one available: put the column's own average where a
value is missing. It needs no model, no package, and one line.

```{python}
imp_mean = gp_py.copy()
imp_mean[num_cols] = gp_py[num_cols].fillna(gp_py[num_cols].mean())

imp_median = gp_py.copy()
imp_median[num_cols] = gp_py[num_cols].fillna(gp_py[num_cols].median())

print("missing left, mean:  ", int(imp_mean[num_cols].isna().sum().sum()))
print("missing left, median:", int(imp_median[num_cols].isna().sum().sum()))
```

`SimpleImputer(strategy="mean")` does the same job through `scikit-learn`, and
that is the form you will meet again in @sec-pipeline-steps, where the imputer
has to be fitted on the training rows alone. `fillna` is used here because this
chapter is about what imputation *does*, not yet about where it belongs.

#### What it did to the spread

Thirty-five values across four columns have just been replaced by four
repeated numbers, so those rows now sit exactly on top of each other in each
column. The standard deviations must fall. Measure it rather than taking it on
trust:

```{python}
comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "sd_before": gp_py[num_cols].std(),
    "sd_mean":   imp_mean[num_cols].std(),
    "sd_median": imp_median[num_cols].std(),
})
comparison["pct_change_mean"] = (
    100 * (comparison.sd_mean - comparison.sd_before) / comparison.sd_before
).round(1)
print(comparison.round(3))
```

Every standard deviation shrank — by 0.3% for `age`, which was missing one
value, and by 4.0% for `systolic_BP`, which was missing fourteen. The size of
the shrinkage tracks how much of the column you invented.

That matters because a standard deviation is what a confidence interval is
built from: impute the mean into 8% of a column and every interval computed
from it afterwards is narrower than the evidence justifies. You have not added
information, but you have made the data look as though you had.

#### Why median, for this column

`BMI` is right-skewed. The mean is pulled upward by the heavier tail; the
median is not.

```{python}
print("BMI mean  :", round(gp_py["BMI"].mean(), 2))
print("BMI median:", round(gp_py["BMI"].median(), 2))
```

A gap of 0.35 of a BMI unit between the two. That is small here because the
skew is mild, and it is the right habit anyway: whichever you choose, every
filled-in value inherits it, so on a strongly skewed column the mean would put
a block of patients at a value most of the cohort sits below.

#### A derived feature does not impute itself

Here is the trap. `BMI` was computed from height and weight **before** the
imputation, so filling the gaps in those two columns does nothing to it — the
derived column still has every gap it started with.

```{python}
print("BMI missing, before imputing:", int(gp_py["BMI"].isna().sum()))
print("BMI missing, after imputing height and weight:",
      int(imp_median["BMI"].isna().sum()))
```

Twenty before, twenty after. Unchanged. The fix is to recompute the derived
column from the filled inputs, and the order matters: impute first, then
derive.

```{python}
imp_median["BMI"] = imp_median.weight_kg / (imp_median.height_cm / 100) ** 2

print("BMI missing, after recomputing:", int(imp_median["BMI"].isna().sum()))
```

Zero. Note what those recomputed BMI values now are: a ratio of two numbers
that were themselves invented. The uncertainty does not announce itself — it is
buried one step further from the data than it was before.

Now colour the imputed rows, because a value at the median does not announce
itself in a histogram either — it lands inside the existing peak and disappears:

```{python}
#| fig-height: 2.6
was_filled = gp_py["weight_kg"].isna() | gp_py["height_cm"].isna()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.6))
bins = np.histogram_bin_edges(imp_median["BMI"].dropna(), bins=30)
ax.hist([imp_median.loc[~was_filled, "BMI"], imp_median.loc[was_filled, "BMI"]],
        bins=bins, stacked=True, color=["grey", "#c0392b"],
        label=["observed", "imputed"])
ax.set_xlabel("BMI")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

Twenty red rows, all of them inside the existing peak. That is the honest
picture, and it is also the warning: had you not kept track of which rows you
filled, nothing in the finished column would tell you. A column of imputed
values looks exactly like a column of measurements. Record which is which — a
`BMI_was_missing` indicator costs one column and keeps the distinction
available to everything downstream.

### Task 1 — What dropping costs

Dropping every incomplete row is the default in a surprising amount of
published analysis, usually silently. Quantify it.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
kept = gp_py.______()
print(kept.shape[0], "of", gp_py.shape[0])
print("lost:", round(100 * (1 - kept.shape[0] / gp_py.shape[0]), 1), "%")

# Did dropping change who is in the data?
print(round(gp_py["diabetes"].mean(), 3))
print(round(kept["______"].mean(), 3))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the method that removes rows containing any missing value.
The last is the `diabetes` column, so you can compare its rate before and after.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
kept = gp_py.dropna()
print(kept.shape[0], "of", gp_py.shape[0])
print("lost:", round(100 * (1 - kept.shape[0] / gp_py.shape[0]), 1), "%")

print(round(gp_py["diabetes"].mean(), 3))
print(round(kept["diabetes"].mean(), 3))
```

A quarter of the cohort goes — 134 rows kept of 180, 25.6% lost. The outcome
rate barely moves, from 0.233 to 0.224, which is what you expect when values
were blanked out at random — and is exactly what you cannot count on when they
were not.
:::
:::

the categorical analogue of the mean, and it has the same defect in a sharper
form: it makes the commonest category commoner, which is precisely the
direction that hides a minority group. Filling a missing practice with
Bournbrook does not record ignorance, it records a guess that favours the

### Stretch

#### Stretch 1 — Iterative imputation

Mean imputation ignores every other column. If a patient's `BMI` is missing but
their `age` and `systolic_BP` are recorded, those two carry information about
the likely `BMI`, and the mean throws it away. Iterative imputation uses it: it
models each column with missing values as a function of the other columns,
predicts the gaps, and repeats — each round using the previous round's filled-in
values — until the estimates settle.

It is a model, and it carries a model's assumptions: that the columns are
related in a way the imputer can represent, and that the missingness does not
itself depend on the value that is missing. For this dataset we happen to know
the second assumption holds, because `data/PROVENANCE.txt` records that values
were blanked out at random after the outcome was generated. On real data you
would not know that, and you would have to argue for it.

`scikit-learn` ships this as
[`IterativeImputer`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.impute.IterativeImputer.html),
still marked experimental, so it has to be enabled explicitly:

```{python}
from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer  # noqa: F401
from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer

imp = IterativeImputer(random_state=42, max_iter=20)
imp_iter = gp_py.copy()
imp_iter[num_cols] = imp.fit_transform(gp_py[num_cols])

print("missing left:", int(imp_iter[num_cols].isna().sum().sum()))
print("iterations run:", imp.n_iter_)
```

Read the iteration count as a diagnostic: with four columns and few gaps there
is very little for the rounds to refine, so the estimates stop moving almost
immediately. On a wide table it would be larger, and an imputer that runs to
`max_iter` without settling is telling you something.

R's equivalent is the [`mice` package](https://amices.org/mice/) — Multivariate
Imputation by Chained Equations — which is not used in this booklet but is the
standard tool there.

compare the imputed values against the ones you deleted. You know the truth,
so you can measure the error — and see how an assumption of random missingness
fails when it is not true.

#### Stretch 3 — Does better imputation buy a better model?
Fit the same classifier on the mean-imputed and the median-imputed data and
compare the test-set accuracy. Form a view before you run it. Then consider how
much of any difference you would be willing to attribute to the imputer, given
that the comparison rests on one split.

### What you can and cannot now claim

You can say the extract is now complete: no model will refuse it, and you can
state exactly which values were observed and which you supplied, and by what
rule.

You cannot say the imputed values are correct. They are estimates, and the mean
and median versions are estimates that ignore every other column in the table.
You also cannot claim your downstream uncertainty is honest — the shrinkage you
measured is still there.

And once again, none of this was done safely. Every mean and median above was
computed from all 180 rows, including the rows you will later use to test. That
is @sec-pipeline-steps.
